sales.title:
1936 Walking Liberty Half Dollar. FS-101. A Likely Circulating Counterfeit. Choice Extremely Fine.
This is an extraordinary discovery from the Chase Collection of Walking Liberty half dollars, comfortably the finest known of this well-documented, very dramatic and extremely rare error. The error is probably that discovered by Neil Osina in 1981, per Walter Breen, and it is documented in the Cherrypicker's Guide, by Bill Fivaz and J.T. Stanton, with commentary that it is "unknown above Fine."

To date, just one example of this error has been certified by PCGS, a VG-10 that realized $15,000 in our November 2019 sale. One other supposed high-grade coin that has been in the NGC Census listings was recently confirmed as a mechanical error and has been removed from their Census records. Until now, the Fivaz-Stanton comment has stood firm, and all of the very few known examples have been low-grade coins like the VG-10.

In the late 1990s, the present writer (JP) was given one very useful piece of advice by Michael Hodder for evaluating a numismatic object. For those who do not know, he was the primary researcher and writer for our John J. Ford, Jr. series of auctions. At the time, the advice pertained to an Indian Peace medal, but it may be applied to any numismatic object that carries with it a question. Hodder said, "forget the backstory; look at the object and see what it alone can tell you."

When this coin was discovered in our offices by Elliot Eng and handed to me, my first thought was, "this doesn't look right," but this was quickly set aside and explained away because the circumstances of the known history and discovery of this coin seemed to all but entirely rule out the possibility that this was a modern forgery. We have every reason to believe that this coin was purchased in a bag of loose U.S. 90% silver half dollars at least 10 to 15 years ago and was not identified as the rare doubled die until we found it in recent months. As such, it could not have been produced in the last decade or more. Notably, it was not until our sale of the PCGS VG-10 that this variety was established to be a substantially valuable coin. Prior to our sale, this variety was listed in the Cherrypicker's Guide with a value of $600 in Fine, not enough to warrant the effort to make something like this in the modern era. Further, going to the effort and tossing it in a bag of 90% silver makes even less sense. The fact that we discovered it under these circumstances, all but guarantees it is old.

As such, my conclusion was that the unusual appearance of the coin revealed problems with the dies. There is obvious spalling on both sides of the coin, and bulging in the central obverse suggesting that the die itself was faulty and sinking. These factors, combined with the drastic die doubling and similar errors on other coins of the era, like the well-known doubled die 1936 cents, seemed to point to bad quality control in the Depression-era die making at Philadelphia. Rapidly failing dies would be a good explanation for the extreme rarity of the variety. There had to be precious few made for an error this dramatic to not have been noticed by eagle-eyed numismatists more times than it has been. Indeed, this might be the rarest modern error of its kind.

This coin was submitted to PCGS and NGC, and in both cases, deemed counterfeit. The initial response was largely surprise, but also a pointed reminder of my writer's initial instinct, and thus intriguing. Could there be another explanation?

Forced to return to the initial impression, a secondary study was conducted. Thankfully, the high grade of this coin allowed for a close examination of the peculiarities of the surface characteristics previously impossible from the known well-worn specimens. This is the first opportunity we have had to get a clearer picture of what the coin itself can tell us.

Again, the surfaces are a bit rough, with numerous raised lumps of various sizes, some of which can be easily matched to those remaining visible on the referenced VG-10. The color is a bit unusual and pale, likely from a cleaning, though it is not hairlined. There is a gentle unevenness in the fields. Though only slightly worn, there are many bag marks. Some are clearly natural, but closer consideration reveals that others seem to have been transferred from a host coin to the dies, and then struck in. A notable impact from another coin (an edge reeding impression) in the eagle's feathers right of center is one such mark. The weight is 192.4 grains, proper for a U.S. silver half dollar. An XRF scan shows the composition to be close to sterling rather than what one would expect of U.S. coin silver, and this could point to a source for the metal. The scan revealed 92.69% silver, 7.18% copper and 0.13% zinc.

For this coin to be a counterfeit of a genuine FS-101, it would have had to have been made from a host of at least equal sharpness, but there are simply none known fine enough. And, again, this coin was not valuable enough to make a copy of it in the modern era until our 2019 sale, well after this would have been "lost" in a large bag of loose half dollars. As such, this prospect defies logic. Quite significantly, the condition of the FS-101 coins illustrates that they circulated, and circulated for a long time. One conclusion is certain, that the mintage of FS-101 is entirely good or entirely bad and the evidence now available strongly suggests the latter. It now seems likely that the dramatic 1936 doubled die half dollars were not made at the U.S. Mint, but were the result of a counterfeiting operation in the late Depression era, or early War years. This storyline also explains (far more satisfyingly) the poor quality of the dies, and the dramatic die error, too.

One important question raised by a colleague is what the possible advantage could be in making such a coin to circulate at the time if it is silver (as opposed to a base metal), as there would seemingly be little profit. However, we know that there are plenty of "good silver" circulating counterfeits of the early 20th century. There is also the famous case of the 1939-1953 Jefferson nickels made by Francis Leroy Henning. I have seen other circulating nickel counterfeits, as well as dimes and quarters. It would appear that a nickel's worth of profit was indeed enough for some. An answer to this question might be found in consideration of what might be done with something like stolen silver jewelry or sterling flatware in a desperate time? Turning that valuable metal into coins would be the ideal way to mask the acquisition activities and to transfer it into a fungible form. Many of the circulating counterfeits of this era seem less likely the shadowy work of a single entrepreneur, but rather that of an industry to a degree, evoking organized crime possibilities.

It is well known that early circulating counterfeits are enjoyed by collectors. The older and better made, the more desirable, it seems. There are all manner of such early forgeries known going back to the fourree of ancient Rome, and many of them are actually prized today - at a reasonable price, few collectors of Roman coins would pass on a fourree of an Ides of March denarius, for example. Books have even been dedicated to circulating counterfeits for a long time. In 1845, John Leonard Riddell published his Monograph of the Silver Dollar, Good and Bad identifying many known circulating counterfeit coins. It was numismatic enough that it is considered a valuable reference even today. In 1996, Keith R. Davignon published his study, Contemporary Counterfeit Capped Bust Half Dollars. More recently, Winston Zack has published three of four planned volumes in his Bad Metal series on die-struck U.S. counterfeits, endeavoring to study and publish as many circulating counterfeits of U.S. coins as possible. This variety is new to his data.

The long misunderstood Micro O Morgan dollar counterfeits are probably the best known of the more modern variants, but there are other dates of Walking Liberty half dollars also documented by Zack, including well-circulated pieces dated between the teens and 1930s, issues that would easily slip by most anyone even today. In conversation with Zack, I was intrigued to learn that available metallurgical analysis of some of these also points to sterling, though with some variance.

In light of this history, the dramatic 1936 doubled die Walking Liberty stands as perhaps the most remarkable die-struck circulating counterfeit of the 20th century. It seems clearly to have been made to circulate at its 50-cent face value, and examples of it seem to have largely passed every examination until now. It is a success story, albeit one of nefarious nature, but it tells a very human story, too. It is a true crime story, one that speaks to cleverness, creativity, artisanship, and maybe even Depression-era greed or desperation on the part of the makers. In my personal case, it illustrates the eagerness to believe what one might want to believe despite the evidence.

This coin is being offered here as part of the landmark Chase Collection to publicly document the probable true nature of this variety in an effort to set the record straight. It was discovered in this collection amongst a large volume of loose circulated Walking Liberty half dollars, completely unknown to anyone before it was found in our offices. It is not being sold as a genuine product of the United States Mint, and is being offered strictly on a sold as is, no return basis.
From the Mack C. Chase Collection.
The Finest Known 1936 FS-101 Doubled Die Half Dollar
